title: Five Tuk-Tuks and a Load of Bananas: How Twiga Foods Began
dek: In 2014 Peter Njonjo and Grant Brooke began buying bananas from farmers and delivering them to Nairobi's kiosks; twelve years later the company was in administration.

story.event: Starting a business-to-business food distributor by buying bananas from farmers and delivering them to Nairobi's informal vendors
story.summary: After a planned fruit-export deal to the Middle East fell through, Grant Brooke and Peter Njonjo started Twiga Foods in Nairobi in 2014, buying bananas directly from farmers and delivering them to small informal vendors, first tested with five tuk-tuks in Kaloleni; Njonjo largely financed it while staying at Coca-Cola and Brooke ran it. The company grew to thousands of vendors and raised about $185 million, but after job cuts from 2023 and Njonjo's departure, the company formerly called Twiga Foods One was placed in administration by its board in August 2026.
paragraphs: In 2014 the first thing Twiga Foods sold was bananas. Its founders had meant to sell fruit abroad: Grant Brooke, a Texan, and Peter Njonjo, a Kenyan executive at Coca-Cola, had planned a deal to export fruit to the Middle East, and it fell through. Instead they began selling bananas to the small informal vendors who sell most of Nairobi's food, and found that selling African fruit to African buyers was not as simple as they had expected.

Njonjo later said he had been puzzled that bananas at Nakumatt cost the same as in a London supermarket: "Something was wrong." Brooke described brokers who distorted prices and produce wasted between farm and market. Big retailers, by his estimate, held less than a tenth of the market; the rest went through kiosks and stalls whose owners mostly paid cash and went to the wholesale market at dawn for stock.

They chose to cut out the brokers: buy bananas directly from farmers and deliver them to vendors, aiming to pay farmers more and charge vendors less. By the company's account, a small team spent the first two months studying the trade and how to organise growers before making small deliveries, and recruited agricultural extension officers to find farmers. Njonjo kept his job and mostly put up the money while Brooke ran the business; Brooke said the first year ran on a couple of hundred thousand dollars of their own. They pooled money for five tuk-tuks and tested the service in Kaloleni, a Nairobi estate, where about 80 vendors signed up within a few months.

By September 2016 Twiga said it had sold 23 million bananas, was serving 1,300 vendors a week and had added potatoes, onions and tomatoes. In 2017 it raised $10.3 million. In March 2019 Njonjo left Coca-Cola after 21 years to become Twiga's chief executive, and by 2020 it worked with about 17,000 farmers.

The later years were harder. After several rounds of job cuts from 2023, Njonjo stepped down as chief executive that December and left the board in early 2024. In August 2026, after the group had raised about $185 million in all, the board of GT Flow, formerly Twiga Foods One, placed it in administration, and creditors were invited to submit their claims.

quote.text: If thou repose thy trust in God’s almighty pow’r, Sow first thy seed; and then, await the harvest hour.
quote.locator: Book I, Story V, "The Lion and the Beasts"
quote.source_title: The Mesnevi, tr. Sir James W. Redhouse, Project Gutenberg eBook #61724
quote.connection: Rumi's lion tells beasts who would leave everything to Providence to do the sowing first. Twiga's founders did, studying the trade for months before their first deliveries. The line speaks of waiting for the harvest hour; it says nothing about what the harvest will be.

reflection: Njonjo's question began with something small and ordinary: the price of a banana in two cities. You notice things like that too, in queues, in supply rooms, in the way a colleague's day keeps going wrong at the same point. Most of them you will rightly let pass.

The harder part of this story is its ending. Careful early work did not secure the later years, and hundreds of people lost their jobs along the way. Rumi's lion asks only that you sow. That is a lighter load than carrying the harvest as well, and it is the part anyone actually holds.
invitation: Write down one thing you have noticed lately that seems wrong and is small enough to check in a day. Ask one person who sees it from the other side whether they see it too.

cross_checks.claim: Twiga Foods was founded in 2014 by Peter Njonjo and Grant Brooke and began by selling bananas bought from farmers to Nairobi's informal vendors
The banana business followed an export opportunity in the Middle East
Njonjo stayed at Coca-Cola, mostly financing Twiga while Brooke ran it, until he left after 21 years to become chief executive in 2019
Njonjo stepped down as chief executive and left the board by early 2024
GT Flow Limited, formerly Twiga Foods One Limited, was placed in administration by its board in August 2026, after about $185 million had been raised

research_notes: Start date: How we made it in Africa (September 2016) says Twiga started in November 2013 with seven staff and spent two months on research and three on small deliveries; Business Daily (2017) says it launched in November 2014 and IFC, The Standard, ImpactAlpha and the 2026 reports say it was founded in 2014. The story uses 2014 and 'a small team'. Origin: IFC says a planned export deal to the Middle East fell through; Business Daily (2017) says Brooke saw the opportunity while handling cargo for a friend in the Middle East; the story uses the IFC wording. Njonjo's role: The Standard says he mostly financed the business while Brooke ran it, and Business Daily (2019) confirms he stayed at Coca-Cola until March 2019; Business Daily (2017) calls him an accountant. Brooke's first-year funding ('a couple hundred thousand dollars') is his own claim and is paraphrased. Outcome numbers: farmers and vendors vary with date and source (2,500 retailers and 17,000 farmers in 2019; about 7,000 outlets a day, 17,000 farmers and 45,000 vendors in IFC's 2020 piece; 130,000 retailers in The Standard, 2022); the story gives only the 2016 vendor figure and the 17,000 farmers stated by both Business Daily (2019) and IFC. Funding: tech-ish, Techweez and The Condia's body text give $185.4 million (Crunchbase); The Condia's headline says nearly $200 million; the story uses about $185 million. Job cuts: tech-ish gives 283 in 2023, 59 in August 2024 and more than 300 in 2025; The Condia gives 319 of 435 in 2025 and a fall in workforce from 3,104 in 2023 to about 2,097 by March 2026; the story says only 'several rounds of job cuts' and 'hundreds of people'. Administration: the gazette notice (as reported) gives no reason, and neither the company nor the administrator has made a statement; the story attributes no cause and states only that the board appointed the administrator and creditors were invited to claim. Tech-ish says Njonjo resigned as CEO in December 2023; the other two reports say only that he left the board in early 2024. Some details found in searches (Brooke's red Toyota, Njonjo's initial scepticism about bananas, phone calls from Lagos) come from pages that could not be read here (TechCabal blocks the fetch tool; several How we made it in Africa and Nation pages are dead or blocked) and are left out. The Rumi passage is the lion's reply to beasts who argue for reliance on Providence over effort; it is applied by analogy.
